A battery radio that fits in your pocket.

Alloy-junction transistor ×3 (amplify) + graphite (carbon resistor) + copper cable (tuning/antenna coil) + Leyden jar (capacitor) + magnet (speaker) + zinc ingot and graphite rod (zinc-carbon battery: zinc can and carbon rod). The goal of chapter 1. No redstone: every part is a real radio part.

It picks one station out of the weak signals from the antenna (tuning), extracts the audio (detection) and amplifies it with transistors to drive the speaker. Unlike tubes there is no warm-up, so it plays at once and the battery lasts.

The Regency TR-1 (USA, 1954, four transistors) was the first commercial transistor radio. Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (later Sony) released the TR-55 in 1955, and its 1957 TR-63 sold worldwide as a 'pocketable' radio.

⚠️ Approximation: the capacitor is a Leyden jar (real radios use small paper, ceramic or electrolytic capacitors). The battery is only its zinc can and carbon rod (the real zinc-carbon cell also needs MnO2 and an ammonium chloride paste, not in the game yet). The speaker cone, ferrite antenna rod and plastic case are omitted. The TR-1 had 4 transistors; here 3.
item.semiconductor-lab.sulfite_liquor.no: A liquid for cooking wood that dissolves the 'glue' (lignin) holding its fibres together.
Sulfur dioxide + slaked lime + water bucket. With 2 logs it makes a digester charge. ⚠ GHS: skin and eye irritant (acidic, smells of sulfur dioxide).
SO2 absorbed in milk of lime gives calcium bisulfite, Ca(HSO3)2. It attaches to lignin and turns it into a water-soluble form (lignosulfonates).
Tilghman in the USA patented the sulfite process in 1867; Ekman in Sweden ran the first mill in 1874.
item.semiconductor-lab.sulfite_liquor.pl: Approximation: liquor strength is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.pulp_charge.note1: Wood and cooking liquor loaded into the vessel. Cooked under pressure, it becomes pulp.
item.semiconductor-lab.pulp_charge.note2: 2 burnable logs + sulfite cooking liquor. In an autoclave (with water, about 130 C and 3 atm or more) it gives 2 wood pulp. With too little pressure it does not cook and comes back unchanged.
item.semiconductor-lab.pulp_charge.note3: Wood is cellulose fibres glued together by lignin. Dissolving only the lignin frees the fibres (cooking, or digestion).
item.semiconductor-lab.pulp_charge.note4: A real digester is a pressure vessel over ten metres tall that cooks wood chips for hours.
item.semiconductor-lab.pulp_charge.place: Approximation: whole logs go in (chipping is skipped).
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_pulp.note1: Cellulose fibres taken from wood. The raw material of paper.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_pulp.note2: Cook a digester charge in an autoclave. 3 -> 3 paper. Raw material for cellulose acetate (the [2-18] RO membrane).
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_pulp.note3: Cellulose is a chain of thousands of glucose units. The chains cling together by hydrogen bonds into strong fibres.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_pulp.note4: From Cai Lun's improved papermaking (105 AD) onward, paper was long made from rags and bark. In the 1840s Keller in Germany ground wood into pulp, and in 1867 Tilghman devised the sulfite process, so paper could be made from wood in huge amounts.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_pulp.placeho: Approximation: bleaching and leftover lignin are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.touch_panel.note1: A screen that reads how much charge it can hold when a finger touches it. Only living things set it off.
item.semiconductor-lab.touch_panel.note2: Assembly bench: ITO glass (transparent electrode) + copper (wiring) + chip that passed NOT (readout). Right-click to read: aimed at a player or animal it shows the change in capacitance (pF); blocks and empty air give nothing.
item.semiconductor-lab.touch_panel.note3: Transparent ITO electrodes run in rows and columns, each crossing holding a little charge. The body conducts through its water, so a nearby finger raises the crossing's capacitance. Gloves or sticks change nothing, so they do not register.
item.semiconductor-lab.touch_panel.note4: Researchers at Britain's Royal Radar Establishment showed an air-traffic-control touch display in 1965; CERN used one in an accelerator control room in 1973. 2007 smartphones spread the multi-touch grid method. ⚠️ Dates being checked.
item.semiconductor-lab.touch_panel.place: Omitted: ⚠️ the size of the change (about 0.5–2 pF) and its dependence on body size are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.fiber_preform.not: A thick glass rod that becomes optical fibre, made of very pure synthetic silica.
4 synthetic quartz + germanium dioxide (raises the core's index). Drawn thin in the oxyhydrogen burner it gives 8 optical fibres (20 dB/km).
Real preforms are made by burning silicon and germanium tetrachloride vapours inside a tube and building up soot (1970s on).
The core's index is about 0.3% higher thanks to germanium, the cladding is pure silica, and that difference traps the light inside.
item.semiconductor-lab.fiber_preform.pla: Approximation: vapour deposition (MCVD etc.) is not modelled; synthetic silica and GeO2 are simply combined.
item.semiconductor-lab.fiber_preform_nat: A preform made from melted natural quartz. Its impurities weaken the light quickly.
4 fused quartz + germanium dioxide. Drawn in the oxyhydrogen burner it gives 8 fibres at 1000 dB/km (the light is almost gone after 100 m).
In the 1960s ordinary glass lost over 1000 dB per km (a factor of 10 to the 100) and was thought useless for communication.
The absorbers were metal impurities such as iron and copper, and water (OH) in the glass. Kao's idea was that removing them would make losses far smaller.
item.semiconductor-lab.optical_fiber.not: A glass thread as thin as a hair. Light inside bounces off its walls and travels a long way.
Draw a preform in the oxyhydrogen burner -> 8. Right-click two blocks to see what percentage of light gets between them (1 block = 1 m). Synthetic silica 20 dB/km, natural quartz 1000 dB/km.

In 1966 Charles Kao showed that glass thread could carry light far once impurities were removed (2009 Nobel Prize in Physics), and in 1970 Corning researchers made fibre below 20 dB/km. Today it is about 0.2 dB/km, and undersea cables carry the world's internet.
With a core index of 1.462 and cladding 1.457, light striking the boundary at more than about 85 deg from the normal is totally reflected, so it stays inside even when the thread bends.
item.semiconductor-lab.optical_fiber.pla: Approximation: no light source (LED, semiconductor laser) exists yet, so the light test has none. Loss is taken as independent of wavelength.
item.semiconductor-lab.optical_fiber.mar: 💡 Light goes in here. It travels by total internal reflection (no escape beyond about %s deg). Right-click another block
item.semiconductor-lab.optical_fiber.sen: 📡 Sent %s m: %s dB/km -> %s dB weaker, %s%% of the light arrives
item.semiconductor-lab.tube_radio.note1: A radio that uses vacuum tubes to make sound louder. Early ones were as big as furniture.
item.semiconductor-lab.tube_radio.note2: Assembly bench: 3 triode tubes + tuning coil + tuning capacitor + speaker + wooden cabinet. Each 10 s listen (right-click) takes 400 J from a lead-acid battery in your inventory (40 W tube heaters).
item.semiconductor-lab.tube_radio.note3: In 1920 KDKA in Pittsburgh began scheduled radio broadcasts, and Japan followed in 1925. Families gathered round big wooden radios to listen.
item.semiconductor-lab.tube_radio.note4: Tubes heat their cathodes red-hot to release electrons, so they take time to warm up and use a lot of power. Transistors need no heating, so radios became small and ran for tens of hours on batteries.
item.semiconductor-lab.tube_radio.placeh: Approximation: there are no broadcast stations, so listening just shows a message. 40 W is a typical value.
item.semiconductor-lab.tube_radio.listen: 📻 The tubes warm up and you hear the broadcast (heaters %s W x %s s = %s J from the battery)
item.semiconductor-lab.tube_radio.no_pow: Silent: the tube heaters need %s J from a lead-acid battery in your inventory
